title: Celestial phenomenon over Nuremberg
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Usually interpreted as a spectacular sun-halo display (parhelia, arcs) described in religious terms.
shape: Spheres, crosses, tubes and a black spear
witnesses: Citizens of Nuremberg
summary: A broadsheet by Hans Glaser describes a dawn "battle" in the sky: globes, crosses and cylinders that moved and fought before falling to the ground with smoke. It is a staple of UFO histories and an example of how atmospheric optics were recorded before modern science.

title: Celestial phenomenon over Basel
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Generally read as atmospheric optics (sun halos, a reddened rising sun) or dust and smoke, described in the religious language of a 16th-century broadsheet.
shape: Many black and fiery spheres
witnesses: Townspeople of Basel (as reported by the broadsheet)
summary: A broadsheet printed in Basel by Samuel Coccius reported that at sunrise on August 7, 1566 many large black spheres were seen racing toward the Sun and seeming to fight one another, some turning red and fiery before fading. It also described a blood-red Sun on the mornings and evenings of late July. Together with Nuremberg 1561, it is one of the best-known early-modern "sky battles".

title: Utsuro-bune — the "hollow ship" of Hitachi
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Historians treat it as folklore: the story appears in several Edo-period collections with conflicting details, and resembles older legends of exiled women set adrift in boats.
shape: Round vessel of wood and iron with glass windows
witnesses: Fishermen (as told in Edo-period accounts)
summary: Several Japanese books of the 1820s–1840s tell how fishermen found a strange round boat washed up on the coast of Hitachi Province in 1803. Inside was a young woman who spoke no known language and clutched a box she would let no one touch. The fishermen pushed the vessel back out to sea. The drawings of the round, windowed ship are often compared with modern "flying saucers".

title: Bonilla observation — objects crossing the Sun
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Camille Flammarion thought Bonilla had seen birds, insects or dust close to the telescope. A 2011 study at UNAM proposed fragments of a comet passing close to Earth. Either way, nothing suggests craft.
shape: Hundreds of dark, fuzzy bodies with tails
witnesses: 1 astronomer (José Bonilla)
summary: On August 12, 1883, José Bonilla, the first director of the Zacatecas observatory, was preparing to observe sunspots when he saw dark objects crossing the face of the Sun. Over two days he counted hundreds of them and took photographs through the telescope. They were published in L'Astronomie in 1886 and are often called the first photographs of unidentified flying objects.

title: Mystery airship wave
place: California to the Midwest and Texas, United States
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: No powered airship capable of such flights existed. Reports are attributed to newspaper hoaxes (some papers invented stories outright), bright planets such as Venus, hot-air "fire balloons" and pranks.
shape: Cigar-shaped "airship" with lights and wings or propellers
witnesses: Thousands, over five months
summary: In November 1896 people in Sacramento and then San Francisco and Oakland reported a lighted airship moving across the night sky. In early 1897 reports spread east through Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, Illinois and Texas, often with tall tales of inventors and crews. The line on the map joins the main clusters of reports in date order. It is a wave of sightings, not one object.

title: Aurora, Texas airship "crash"
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Widely regarded as a newspaper hoax written to draw attention to a town in decline. Later digs, metal samples and a search of the cemetery found nothing unusual.
shape: Airship
witnesses: Newspaper account by S. E. Haydon
summary: On April 19, 1897 the Dallas Morning News printed a report from Aurora. It said an airship had struck Judge J. S. Proctor's windmill around 6 a.m. and exploded, and that the pilot, "not an inhabitant of this world", had been buried in the town cemetery. It came at the very end of the 1896–97 airship wave and has been re-investigated many times since the 1970s.

title: Great Meteor Procession
place: Toronto, Ontario, on a path from Saskatchewan to Bermuda
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The astronomer Clarence Chant collected more than a hundred reports and found they all lay along one great-circle arc, with no radiant. He concluded the fireballs were the pieces of a small, short-lived natural satellite of the Earth, breaking up as it grazed the atmosphere. Later studies by John O’Keefe and others agreed.
shape: A procession of 40 to 60 slow fireballs in groups, with a bright tail-less body at the rear
witnesses: More than a hundred reports from Canada, the northeastern United States, Bermuda and ships at sea
duration: Each fireball 30–40 seconds; the whole procession about five minutes
summary: At about 9 p.m. on February 9, 1913, people across Canada and the northeastern United States saw between 40 and 60 bright, slow fireballs cross the sky from horizon to horizon on practically the same path. They came in groups, threw out sparks and were followed by a clear, tail-less light “like a big star”; some witnesses heard rumbling. The same procession was reported from Bermuda and from ships as far south as Brazil, a ground track of more than 11,000 km. Much of the populous Northeast was under cloud, so most of the reports came from rural Canada. From the sound reports William Pickering put the meteors at about 56 km up. O’Keefe later named them the Cyrillids, after the feast day of St. Cyril of Alexandria, February 9.

title: Brown Mountain lights
place: Brown Mountain, Pisgah National Forest, North Carolina
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: In 1922, U.S. Geological Survey geologist George R. Mansfield used maps and an alidade to show the lights were train headlights, car headlights and brush fires in the valleys beyond the ridge. A 1913 USGS look had already pointed to locomotive headlights.
shape: Lights rising above the ridge
witnesses: Visitors to overlooks such as Wiseman's View
summary: In 1913 the Charlotte Observer reported lights rising over Brown Mountain in the Blue Ridge, during the years when electric lighting and railways were reaching the area. Two U.S. Geological Survey investigations followed. Legends of lights "seen by the Cherokee" were added later. The lights are still watched from roadside overlooks.

title: Battle of Los Angeles
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Navy attributed the alarm to "war nerves" after a Japanese submarine shelled the Ellwood oil field the night before; a weather balloon is thought to have started the barrage. The famous Los Angeles Times photo was heavily retouched.
shape: Unidentified targets / searchlight cone
witnesses: Thousands; coastal anti-aircraft batteries
duration: About 2 hours, with the barrage lasting about 1 hour
summary: Less than three months after Pearl Harbor, radar and observers reported an unidentified target approaching Los Angeles. Anti-aircraft batteries fired more than 1,400 shells into the night sky while searchlights converged over Santa Monica and Culver City. No aircraft was downed and no bombs fell; falling shrapnel and heart attacks caused deaths on the ground.

title: Foo fighters — 415th Night Fighter Squadron
explanation: Proposed explanations include St. Elmo’s fire, ball lightning, flares and misidentified aircraft; none fits all reports.
shape: Balls of orange or red light pacing aircraft
witnesses: USAAF night-fighter crews
summary: Crews of the U.S. 415th Night Fighter Squadron repeatedly reported glowing balls of light that followed their Beaufighters over the Rhine. They called them "foo fighters"; similar reports came from Allied and Axis crews in Europe and the Pacific.

title: Ängelholm landing report
explanation: There is only one witness, and his account grew over the years. The traces he pointed to were never independently documented, and the story is not corroborated.
shape: Disc landed in a forest clearing
witnesses: 1 (Gösta Carlsson)
summary: Businessman Gösta Carlsson said that in May 1946, during the Swedish ghost-rocket summer, he came upon a disc-shaped craft standing in a clearing in the Kronoskogen forest and was warned off by its occupants. In 1972 he built a small memorial at the spot, marking where he said the craft had stood. It is now a local landmark.

title: Ghost rockets — Lake Kölmjärv
explanation: Swedish, British and U.S. investigators found no Soviet rockets; many of ~2,000 reports were meteors, but around 200 radar returns and several crashes into lakes were never explained.
shape: Rocket- or cigar-shaped objects
witnesses: Farmer Knut Lindbäck and others; Swedish military
summary: During 1946 Scandinavian observers logged about 2,000 sightings of rocket-like objects. On 19 July a farmer watched one plunge into Lake Kölmjärv; the Swedish Army searched the lake for two weeks and found only a fresh crater in the lakebed.

title: Maury Island incident
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Investigators judged it a hoax: the “debris” was ordinary slag and rock, and the photographs showed nothing. The two men involved later gave conflicting accounts.
shape: Six doughnut-shaped craft, one said to be damaged
witnesses: Harold Dahl, his son and a colleague, Fred Crisman (claimed)
summary: A harbour patrolman, Harold Dahl, said six large doughnut-shaped craft circled above his boat off Maury Island in the afternoon of June 21, 1947, three days before Kenneth Arnold’s famous sighting. One craft was said to be damaged and to shed hot metallic slag that burned his son and killed the dog. Dahl’s employer, Fred Crisman, backed the story, and the case was investigated by Kenneth Arnold and by two Army Air Forces intelligence officers. It is remembered as one of the first reported UFO hoaxes, and for the first story of a “man in black” silencing a witness.

title: Kenneth Arnold — "flying saucers" over Mount Rainier
explanation: Project Blue Book listed the sighting as a mirage. Other proposals include a fireball, pelicans and reflections; none has been widely accepted.
shape: Nine thin, crescent / convex objects in echelon
witnesses: 1 pilot (Kenneth Arnold)
summary: Private pilot Kenneth Arnold, searching for a crashed Marine C-46 in his CallAir A-2, saw nine bright objects in a chain flying south past Mount Rainier. He timed them from Rainier to Mount Adams — roughly 50 miles — in 1 minute 42 seconds, implying well over 1,200 mph. The press coverage coined "flying saucer" and began the modern UFO era.

title: Rhodes photographs — Phoenix
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Air Force file records that Dr. Irving Langmuir, told a thunderstorm had just passed, judged the object to be paper carried up by the wind; photographers it consulted doubted the pictures. A historian has since argued they were faked.
shape: Heel-shaped disc with a hole in the centre
witnesses: 1 (William A. Rhodes)
summary: Amateur astronomer and inventor William Rhodes said he heard a "whoosh" like a jet, grabbed his camera and took two photographs of a heel-shaped object circling over his home. The Arizona Republic printed them on July 9, 1947. The FBI and Army counter-intelligence took the negatives, and the case became "Incident 40" in the Air Force files, one of the first UFO photographs to be studied officially.

title: Roswell debris recovery
place: Foster homestead near Corona, New Mexico
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The U.S. Air Force reports of 1994–1997 identified the debris as a Project Mogul balloon train (NYU Flight 4) launched from Alamogordo Army Air Field to listen for Soviet nuclear tests, and later "alien body" stories as conflations with 1950s dummy drops.
shape: Debris of foil, rubber, sticks and tape
witnesses: Rancher Mac Brazel; 509th Bomb Group officers
summary: Rancher W. W. "Mac" Brazel found a field of debris on the Foster ranch. On July 8, 1947, Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a "flying disc"; within a day the Army re-described it as a weather balloon. Interest revived in the late 1970s, and the Air Force published two reports concluding the debris came from Project Mogul.

title: Mantell UFO incident
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project Blue Book (Ruppelt) concluded Mantell was most likely chasing a classified Navy Skyhook balloon, probably launched from Clinton County AFB, Ohio. Mantell climbed above 25,000 ft without oxygen and lost consciousness.
shape: Large bright object, "ice-cream cone" / metallic
witnesses: Godman tower staff, police, 4 P-51 pilots
summary: Kentucky Highway Patrol reports of a large circular object near Maysville reached Godman Field, where tower staff saw it too. A flight of four Kentucky Air National Guard P-51 Mustangs was asked to investigate. Capt. Thomas Mantell kept climbing after his wingmen levelled off, blacked out without oxygen and died when his P-51 crashed on a farm south of Franklin.

title: Chiles–Whitted encounter
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project Blue Book formally attributed the sighting to a bright meteor (bolide) in 1959.
shape: Wingless cigar with two rows of glowing "windows"
witnesses: 2 Eastern Air Lines pilots, 1 passenger
summary: Eastern Air Lines captain Clarence Chiles and co-pilot John Whitted, flying a DC-3 at about 5,000 ft, saw a glowing torpedo-shaped object rush past their right side and pull up into the clouds. Project Sign took the report so seriously it contributed to the "Estimate of the Situation", which General Vandenberg rejected.

title: Gorman dogfight
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Air Force concluded in 1949 that Gorman had chased a lighted weather balloon.
shape: Small blinking ball of light
witnesses: P-51 pilot, Piper Cub crew, tower controller
summary: North Dakota Air National Guard pilot George Gorman stayed aloft in his P-51 after his flight landed and saw a blinking light that no traffic accounted for. He chased it through turns and steep climbs over Hector Airport until he lost it about 25 miles south-west of Fargo. Tower controllers and a Piper Cub crew also watched the light.

title: Clyde Tombaugh’s Las Cruces sighting
explanation: Tombaugh never said it was a spacecraft. At the time he wrote that he doubted it was a reflection of anything on the ground, as nothing like it had appeared before or since. Later he thought the most likely cause was a reflection from an inversion layer, given how faint the lights were and how they faded as they moved away from the zenith.
shape: Six to eight faint, bluish-green rectangles of light in a geometrical group
witnesses: Clyde Tombaugh, discoverer of Pluto, his wife and his mother-in-law
duration: About 3 seconds (his wife saw it for about 1½ seconds)
summary: On the night of August 20, 1949, Clyde Tombaugh, who had found Pluto nineteen years earlier and was then working on missile tracking at White Sands, was sitting in his back yard in Las Cruces with his wife and mother-in-law. He saw a group of six to eight faint, bluish-green rectangles of light, in a fixed arrangement, pass overhead from the north-west and fade as they went toward the south-eastern horizon. “I was so unprepared for such a strange sight that I was really petrified with astonishment,” he wrote. He is probably the most eminent astronomer to have reported a UFO, and he went on to support the scientific study of them, while saying he could not take interstellar visitors seriously.

title: McMinnville (Trent) photographs
place: Trent farm near Sheridan / McMinnville, Oregon
explanation: The Condon Committee called it one of the few cases where the evidence was consistent with the witnesses’ account; skeptics (Sheaffer, Maccabee critics, later photogrammetry) argue it was a small model hung from overhead wires.
shape: Metallic disc with a raised "mast"
witnesses: Paul and Evelyn Trent
summary: Evelyn Trent saw a metallic disc moving slowly over the farm; her husband Paul took two photographs with a box camera. The images ran in LIFE magazine and became among the most analysed UFO photos ever taken.

title: Mariana film, Great Falls
explanation: The Air Force suggested reflections from two F-94 jets landing nearby; later analyses dispute the geometry.
shape: Two bright spinning discs
witnesses: Nicholas Mariana and his secretary
summary: Great Falls Electrics baseball manager Nicholas Mariana filmed two bright objects crossing the sky with his 16 mm camera. The Air Force returned the film with frames missing; the case was studied by Project Blue Book, the Robertson Panel and the Condon Committee.

title: U.S. Navy R5D — object over the North Atlantic
explanation: The Blue Book record card gives its consulting astronomer's view that the crew saw an astronomical display. The crew said it was a solid object that came up to meet them.
shape: Huge yellowish glow, semicircular
witnesses: Navy flight crew and passengers
summary: A U.S. Navy R5D transport flying toward Newfoundland at about 10,000 ft saw a yellowish glow, like a fire, ahead and below. It rushed toward the aircraft and grew very large and bright, with a semicircular shape. Then it turned 180° and vanished over the horizon at great speed. The Air Force logged the report at 49°50′N 50°03′W. Crew member Lt. Graham Bethune later described it publicly.

title: Lubbock Lights
explanation: Project Blue Book’s Edward Ruppelt concluded the lights were probably plovers reflecting street lights; the photos themselves were never shown to be faked.
shape: V / arc formation of 15–30 bluish lights
witnesses: Texas Tech professors, residents
duration: Seconds per pass; repeated over weeks
summary: Starting on 25 August 1951, three Texas Tech professors saw arcs of faint lights sweep silently overhead several times. On 30–31 August, 18-year-old Carl Hart Jr. photographed a V-shaped formation of lights from his backyard.

title: Fort Monmouth radar and T-33 sighting
place: Fort Monmouth and the Jersey Shore, New Jersey
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Blue Book's record card: "Extensive investigation revealed that the target on 10 Sept was caused by a balloon. Targets on 11 September were attributed to anomalous propagation."
shape: Fast radar target; silver disc seen from a T-33
witnesses: Army radar operators; two Air Force pilots
summary: During a demonstration at the Army Signal Corps radar school at Fort Monmouth, an operator picked up a low target moving too fast for the automatic tracking. Minutes later, the crew of an Air Force T-33 over Point Pleasant reported a silver disc below them and dived after it. More radar targets followed the next day. The case alarmed the Pentagon and led the Air Force to reorganise Project Grudge, which became Project Blue Book.

title: Wonsan and Sunchon B-29 sightings
explanation: No explanation was ever settled. Air Force Lt. Gen. Otto Weyland said that “we can’t say there’s nothing to it” but that without more data a conclusive answer could not be expected, and he doubted that jet aircraft were responsible.
shape: Orange sphere or disc, with occasional blue flames
witnesses: Two B-29 crews from different squadrons
duration: Five minutes or more at Wonsan; about a minute at Sunchon
summary: Around midnight on the night of January 29, 1952, during the Korean War, the rear gunner and the central fire-control gunner of a B-29 Superfortress at 20,000 feet over Wonsan saw an orange, globe-shaped light about three feet across that stayed near the bomber for five minutes or more. A second B-29 from a different squadron, hundreds of miles away at Sunchon, reported a lighted orange sphere that followed it for about a minute on the way back to base. The two reports were made independently by trained aircrew over hostile territory, and the story was widely published in February 1952. Air Force UFO experts have argued that the wide publicity it received helped feed the 1952 wave, which ended over Washington, D.C.

title: Tremonton, Utah film
explanation: Navy photo analysts could not identify the objects; the 1953 Robertson Panel suggested seagulls reflecting sunlight. The film was re-released in 2026 as PURSUE record DOW-UAP-PR159.
shape: About a dozen bright objects milling in the sky
witnesses: Navy Chief Warrant Officer Delbert C. Newhouse and family
summary: Driving about seven miles north of Tremonton, Navy photographer Delbert Newhouse stopped and filmed a group of bright objects with his Bell & Howell 16 mm camera. The Navy’s Photographic Interpretation Laboratory spent over 1,000 man-hours on it and ruled out aircraft and birds; the Robertson Panel disagreed.

title: Nash–Fortenberry sighting
place: Chesapeake Bay near Newport News, Virginia
explanation: Listed as "unknown" by Project Blue Book. Menzel suggested haze-distorted ground lights or fireflies; others a mirage of Venus.
shape: Eight glowing red-orange discs in echelon
witnesses: 2 Pan Am pilots; independent ground witnesses
summary: Pan American pilots William Nash and William Fortenberry, flying a DC-4 at 8,000 ft toward Norfolk, saw eight glowing discs race in formation below them, flip on edge and reverse direction, then climb west out of sight. Blue Book classified the case as unknown.

title: Washington, D.C. radar-visual sightings
explanation: The Air Force attributed the radar returns to temperature inversions; radar controllers involved rejected that explanation. The widely published "Capitol UFO" photo shows lens flares.
evidence: radar | pilot-witness | military-witness | multiple-witnesses | official-document | photo
shape: Radar blips; orange-red lights
witnesses: Air traffic controllers, airline and fighter pilots
summary: On consecutive Saturday nights, controllers at Washington National Airport and Andrews AFB tracked unknown targets over the capital — including the prohibited airspace over the White House and Capitol — while airline pilots saw lights where radar showed them. F-94 jets scrambled from New Castle AFB, Delaware; one pilot said lights surrounded his aircraft. The Pentagon held its largest press conference since WWII.

title: Flatwoods "monster"
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Investigator Joe Nickell concluded the light was a meteor seen over three states that evening, the pulsing red glow an aircraft beacon, and the "monster" a barn owl on a branch, magnified by fear. The witnesses' nausea fits fright and the smoke of the fire.
shape: Bright light; tall figure with a spade-shaped hood
witnesses: 7 (the May brothers, Kathleen May, Eugene Lemon and others)
summary: Just after 7 p.m. three boys saw a bright light cross the sky and come down on the Fisher farm. They climbed the hill with Kathleen May, National Guardsman Eugene Lemon and two other boys. At the top they saw a pulsing red light, and in Lemon's flashlight beam a tall figure with a glowing face and a spade-shaped hood. It hissed, and they fled. Several later felt sick. A bright meteor was reported over Maryland, Pennsylvania and West Virginia that same evening.

title: RAF Topcliffe disc — Exercise Mainbrace
shape: Silver disc, rotating
witnesses: Flt Lt John Kilburn and RAF aircrew on the ground
summary: During NATO's Exercise Mainbrace, RAF aircrew at Topcliffe watched a silver, disc-shaped object following a Meteor jet as it came down to land at nearby Dishforth. The object descended, swinging "like a pendulum", hovered and rotated. It then shot away westward at high speed. The report made front pages and was raised in Parliament years later.

title: Oloron-Sainte-Marie "angel hair"
explanation: Most researchers attribute "angel hair" falls to silk from migrating ballooning spiders, common in autumn. The Oloron filaments dissolved and no sample was analysed.
shape: White cylinder with a train of smaller "saucers" in pairs
witnesses: Jean-Yves Prigent of the Oloron lycée, his family and townspeople
summary: Around midday, residents of Oloron-Sainte-Marie saw a cottony white cylinder tilted at 45°, drifting slowly across a nearly cloudless sky. Around it were about thirty smaller objects moving in zig-zagging pairs. Long white filaments ("angel hair") fell from them onto roofs, trees and wires, then turned to jelly and vanished. A similar event followed at Gaillac ten days later.

title: Little Rissington Meteor encounter
place: Over Gloucestershire from RAF Little Rissington
shape: Three white, perfectly circular discs
witnesses: Flt Lt Michael Swiney and Lt David Crofts (Royal Navy)
summary: An instructor from the Central Flying School and a Royal Navy trainee broke through cloud at 12,000 ft in a Meteor T.7 and saw three white, circular objects far above, which they first took for parachutes. They climbed toward 35,000 ft, but the objects crossed their path from left to right and disappeared in a fraction of a second. Radar at Gloucester reported three objects, two Meteor F.8s were scrambled, and Southern Sector radar logged targets heading east at great speed.

title: West Malling Vampire sighting
explanation: In Parliament, the Secretary of State for Air said the object was "a weather balloon". The crew did not accept this.
shape: Bright object
witnesses: RAF aircrew Terry Johnson and Geoffrey Smythe
summary: Two RAF aircrew flying a de Havilland Vampire over West Malling reported an unidentified object. The report reached the House of Commons, where the Air Minister called it a weather balloon. Another MP raised it again the next day.

title: Kinross F-89 disappearance over Lake Superior
place: Lake Superior, off the Keweenaw Peninsula, Michigan
explanation: The Air Force said the target was a Royal Canadian Air Force C-47 flying off course and that the F-89 probably crashed after the pilot became disoriented (vertigo). The RCAF denied any intercept took place, and no wreckage of the F-89 has ever been found.
shape: Unidentified radar target
witnesses: Ground-control radar operators
summary: Air defense radar picked up an unidentified target over the restricted airspace near the Soo Locks. An F-89C Scorpion was scrambled from Kinross AFB, flown by 1st Lt. Felix Moncla with radar operator 2nd Lt. Robert Wilson. Ground controllers watched the fighter close on the target over Lake Superior at about 8,000 ft, until the two returns merged into one. The F-89 never answered again, and neither the aircraft nor its crew was ever found.

title: BOAC Stratocruiser paced by seven objects
place: Gulf of St. Lawrence, near Sept-Îles, Quebec
explanation: Suggested explanations include a mirage or other optical effect in the evening sky; none has been generally accepted.
shape: One large dark object and six smaller ones
witnesses: Captain James Howard, First Officer Lee Boyd, crew and passengers
summary: BOAC Flight 510-196, a Boeing Stratocruiser from New York to London via Goose Bay, was cruising at 19,000 ft when the crew saw a large dark object and six smaller ones keeping pace a few miles off the port side. They held station for 18 minutes as the crew and passengers watched. Goose Bay sent up a USAF F-94. As it approached, the small objects seemed to merge into the large one, which shrank and disappeared. Captain Howard was interviewed on the BBC days later.

title: Quarouble railway encounter — Marius Dewilde
explanation: The marks on the sleepers were real, and an investigator thought they could be landing struts. But there was one witness, who had suffered a head injury the year before and later had nervous disorders, and the air police and gendarmes found no footprints or other proof.
shape: Dark mass on the railway with two or more small figures
witnesses: Marius Dewilde, a 34-year-old metalworker
summary: On the night of September 10, 1954, Marius Dewilde, living beside a level crossing on the Saint-Amand–Blanc-Misseron line, went into his yard after his dog barked. He saw a dark mass on the tracks and two small figures, about a metre tall with large heads like glass helmets, heading for it. When he approached, a bright light left him unable to move; the object rose and vanished to the west. Air police inspectors found symmetrical dents in the wooden sleepers at five places and displaced ballast, and one of them said the marks might fit landing struts. It became one of the best-known cases of the 1954 wave of sightings in France.

title: Salandin near-miss over Southend
shape: Two circular objects, one silver and one gold
witnesses: 1 (Flt Lt James Salandin, No. 604 Squadron)
summary: Flt Lt James Salandin of the Royal Auxiliary Air Force was climbing through 16,000 ft over Southend in a Meteor F.8 from North Weald when two circular objects, one silver and one gold, came toward him. The silver one came head-on, filling his windscreen, and he only narrowly avoided a collision. He reported it on landing.

title: Florence stadium sighting
explanation: Proposed explanations include migrating spiders' silk (angel hair) catching the sunlight. A sample analysed by University of Florence chemists was reported to contain boron, silicon, calcium and magnesium, which does not fit spider silk. The sample was not preserved.
shape: Egg- or cigar-shaped objects; falling silvery filaments
witnesses: About 10,000 spectators and the players
summary: During a match between Fiorentina and Pistoiese, the crowd and players stopped to stare at objects crossing the sky over the stadium. Witnesses described slow-moving "eggs" or fast "cigars" that stopped dead. Silvery filaments drifted down onto the ground and dissolved when touched. The same day two shining objects were reported over Venice, and sightings followed across Tuscany.

title: Kelly–Hopkinsville encounter
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project Blue Book listed the case as a hoax. Investigators have since suggested great horned owls, which defend their nests aggressively at night and have eyes that shine in torchlight, seen by frightened people after a meteor passed overhead.
shape: Light in the sky; small, glowing "goblins"
witnesses: 11 members of the Sutton and Lankford households
summary: Around 7 p.m. Billy Ray Taylor said he saw a bright light land in a gully behind the Sutton farmhouse. Over the next hours the family reported small, silvery creatures with large eyes and ears approaching the house, and they fired guns at them repeatedly. At about 11 p.m. they drove to the Hopkinsville police. Officers found bullet holes but nothing else. The family said the creatures came back after the police left.

title: Lakenheath–Bentwaters radar-visual case
explanation: The Condon Report judged "the probability that at least one genuine UFO was involved appears to be fairly high"; others propose anomalous radar propagation, meteors and stars.
shape: Fast radar targets; luminous objects
witnesses: USAF radar operators and ground crew; RAF Venom crews
summary: Radar at USAF-run RAF Bentwaters tracked targets at thousands of miles per hour coming in from the sea. Lakenheath’s ground personnel then saw luminous objects, and RAF de Havilland Venom night fighters were scrambled. One pilot reported locking on before the target appeared behind him; radar showed it following the fighter.

title: West Freugh radar incident
place: RAF West Freugh, near Stranraer, Scotland
shape: Radar echo "as large as a ship"
witnesses: Radar operators at West Freugh and Ardwell
summary: Radar at West Freugh tracked a very large target hanging almost stationary at about 50,000 ft over the Irish Sea for ten minutes. It then rose vertically to about 70,000 ft and moved off. A second radar at Ardwell tracked it too. Operators said it made a turn no aircraft could make and gave an echo bigger than a normal aircraft, like a ship.

title: Milton Torres — ordered to fire on a UFO
place: Over East Anglia, from RAF Manston
explanation: One suggestion is that the target was a radar-spoofing test by U.S. electronic-warfare units (Project Palladium). This has not been confirmed, and the MoD found no record of the incident.
shape: Radar return the size of an aircraft carrier
witnesses: 1 (Lt Milton Torres, USAF); ground-control radar
summary: Lt Milton Torres, a USAF F-86D pilot at RAF Manston, was scrambled after ground radar tracked a large target over East Anglia. He was ordered to fire a full salvo of 24 rockets at it and got a radar lock at 32,000 ft. He said the return was as big as an aircraft carrier. Before he could fire, it accelerated off his scope at an estimated Mach 10 or more. He said a man in civilian clothes later warned him not to talk. His account was published in the UK National Archives UFO files in 2008.

title: Marfa lights
place: Mitchell Flat, east of Marfa, Texas
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Observers from the University of Texas at Dallas (2004) and a study over 2000–2008 concluded that most lights are car headlights on U.S. 67, distorted by layers of warm and cool desert air, along with ranch lights and campfires.
shape: Glowing orbs that split, merge and drift
witnesses: Visitors to the viewing area, nightly
summary: Lights seen on the desert toward the Chinati Mountains, south-west of the Marfa Lights Viewing Area on U.S. 90, are said to bob, split, merge and change colour. Local lore traces them to a cowhand in 1883, but the first published account is a 1957 Coronet magazine article. The town now promotes them to tourists.

title: RB-47 radar–ECM–visual encounter
explanation: Condon Report Case 5 concluded the crew’s recollections were "not adequate to allow identification"; skeptics have proposed a mix of airliner lights and ground radar. Physicist James McDonald considered it among the strongest cases.
shape: Intense white / red light; 2.8–3 GHz radar-like signal
witnesses: 6-man USAF RB-47H crew; ground radar operators
summary: An RB-47H electronic-reconnaissance jet of the 55th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing was paced across Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas by a source seen visually by the pilots, detected by the ECM operators’ direction-finding gear, and painted by ground radar at the same position. The source blinked off on all three channels at once, then reappeared.

title: Ubatuba magnesium fragments
explanation: The fragments are real and were analysed, but the story of their origin rests on a letter from an unnamed reader. Later isotope analyses found ordinary terrestrial magnesium, and sceptics regard the tale as a hoax.
shape: Disc that exploded over the sea (as told)
witnesses: A fisherman and friends (reported in a letter)
summary: On September 14, 1957 the Rio de Janeiro columnist Ibrahim Sued printed a letter, with three small pieces of white metal, from a reader who said he had watched a disc explode over the sea near Ubatuba and had picked up fragments. A laboratory of Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture and a second spectrographic analysis found the metal to be extremely pure magnesium. Ufologists, among them James Harder, argued that purity that high was hard to make at the time; later analyses of the isotopes gave normal Earth ratios, and the origin of the pieces remains unproven.

title: Antônio Vilas-Boas abduction claim
place: São Francisco de Sales, Minas Gerais, Brazil
explanation: It is one account by one man, first told months afterwards. The researcher Peter Rogerson doubts it, noting that a similar story ran in the magazine O Cruzeiro in November 1957, before Vilas-Boas first reported his, and arguing that he may have borrowed details from it and from the contactee George Adamski.
shape: Circular or egg-shaped craft with a rotating cupola
witnesses: Antônio Vilas-Boas, a 23-year-old farmer (the only witness)
summary: Antônio Vilas-Boas, a farmer working at night in a field, said that on the night of October 15–16, 1957 a circular craft landed near him and that five-foot beings in grey coveralls seized him, took him aboard, took blood from his chin and exposed him to an unknown gas. He also described a sexual encounter with a female being, and said the whole episode lasted about four hours. In February 1958 Dr. Olavo Fontes of Brazil’s National School of Medicine examined him and concluded he had been exposed to a large dose of radiation, with mild radiation sickness: pains, nausea, headaches, loss of appetite and skin lesions that appeared over the following months. It is often cited as one of the earliest well-known abduction stories, and it is widely doubted.

title: Levelland vehicle-stopping reports
explanation: Project Blue Book attributed the reports to ball lightning / an electrical storm; weather records showed drizzle but little lightning.
shape: Glowing egg-shaped object, 100–200 ft
witnesses: 15+ motorists, sheriff, fire chief
summary: Over roughly three hours, motorists on several highways around Levelland independently reported a glowing, egg-shaped object on or over the road; each said their engine and headlights died until it left. Sheriff Weir Clem and Fire Chief Ray Jones saw lights as well.

title: White Sands military police patrols
place: White Sands Proving Ground (up-range), New Mexico
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project Blue Book concluded the first patrol saw the half-full Moon through broken cloud, with the drifting cloud creating the apparent motion, and the second saw Venus, then near its greatest brilliance.
shape: Reddish-orange, egg-shaped light
witnesses: Two U.S. Army military police patrols
summary: Hours after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2, and on the same night as the Levelland sightings in Texas, two Army MP patrols in jeeps reported lights up-range. At about 2:30 a.m. the first saw a brilliant, reddish-orange egg-shaped light hover for about three minutes, then descend and disappear. That evening a second patrol saw a glowing object that climbed until it looked like a star. The reports reached the newspapers during the November 1957 wave. Air Force investigators found the young soldiers had talked over their sightings before reporting them.

title: Fort Itaipu sentries burned
place: Fort Itaipu, Praia Grande, São Paulo
shape: Bright orange light descending from the sky
witnesses: 2 sentries; garrison woken by the power failure
summary: In the early hours, the day after Sputnik 2, two sentries at the coastal Fort Itaipu saw a bright orange light descend and stop above the fort. They said a wave of intense heat followed and both collapsed with burns. The fort's electricity failed, including the emergency circuits. Brazilian military investigators interviewed the soldiers, and American officials were reported to have joined them.

title: Kirtland Air Force Base tower sighting
place: Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Capt. Shere of Ent AFB, who interviewed the controllers for Project Blue Book, found nothing a small private aircraft could not do and concluded that was what they saw; the radar returns matched a small plane. The Condon Report agreed, suggesting a pilot who had strayed onto the military field by mistake. The physicist James McDonald, who later spoke to the controllers, said they found the explanation amusing.
shape: Egg-shaped object, 15–20 ft tall, with a single white light at its base
witnesses: CAA tower controllers R. M. Kaser and E. G. Brink
duration: About a minute in view; about 20 minutes on radar
summary: At about 10:45 p.m. on November 4, 1957, in the week of the Levelland sightings, two Civil Aeronautics Administration controllers in the tower at Kirtland AFB saw a white light cross the airfield eastward. A dark object then came down steeply near the end of runway 26 and crossed the field a few tens of feet up. Through binoculars it looked egg-shaped, 15 to 20 feet tall, with one white light at its base. It hovered within 3,000 feet of the tower for up to a minute, moved east to the base boundary and climbed fast into the overcast. Albuquerque Radar Approach Control tracked a target that turned south, circled near the low-frequency range station, hovered over the outer marker, then followed a departing C-46 for about 14 miles before returning to the marker and fading. Radar contact lasted about 20 minutes.

title: Trindade Island photographs
explanation: The Brazilian Navy examined the negatives and did not declare a hoax; skeptics argue photographer Almiro Baraúna faked them.
shape: Saturn-like disc with a ring
witnesses: Crew and scientists aboard the Almirante Saldanha
summary: As the Navy survey ship Almirante Saldanha prepared to leave Trindade during the International Geophysical Year, people on deck saw a ringed disc approach from the east, pass over Desejado Peak, turn sharply and leave to the north-west. Photographer Almiro Baraúna took four frames; President Kubitschek allowed their release.

title: Father Gill’s sightings at Boianai
explanation: Sceptics, among them Donald Menzel, identified the first bright light as Venus and later lights as other celestial objects. Several witnesses and Gill’s own written report, signed by 25 of them, describe more than a distant light.
shape: Disc with figures on top; bright lights
witnesses: Rev. William Booth Gill and some 38 others, most of them villagers
summary: On the evening of June 26, 1959 the Anglican missionary William Booth Gill saw a bright white light to the north-west of the Boianai Mission. About 38 other people, mostly staff and villagers of the mission, joined him as a large disc appeared above the station, with four figures seen moving on top of it. Gill waved and, he said, the figures waved back. The sightings continued the next night. Gill wrote a report signed by 25 witnesses, and the case was studied by the Royal Australian Air Force and by J. Allen Hynek, who counted it among the best close encounters of the third kind of its time.

title: Red Bluff — California Highway Patrol sighting
place: Red Bluff area, Tehama County, California
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Air Force concluded the Red Bluff sightings were due to atmospheric refraction, most probably of the planet Mars rising, with a strong temperature inversion and a layer of forest-fire smoke adding to the effect.
shape: Football-shaped object with red lights at each end
witnesses: CHP officers Charles Carson and Stanley Scott; sheriff's deputies
summary: Two California Highway Patrol officers thought they were about to see an airliner crash when a large object dropped toward the road ahead of them. At about 100–200 ft it stopped, reversed and climbed. They watched it for more than two hours as it moved about the sky, swept a red beam over the area and caused radio interference. Deputies at the Tehama County sheriff's office also saw lights. Similar reports came from across northern California that week.

title: Betty and Barney Hill
place: U.S. Route 3, Franconia Notch to Indian Head, New Hampshire
explanation: The Air Force file notes that Jupiter was low in the south-west and would have set about when the object disappeared, and that there was a strong temperature inversion. The abduction story emerged only under hypnosis in 1964. The psychiatrist, Dr. Benjamin Simon, believed it was a fantasy that grew out of Betty's dreams.
shape: Pancake-shaped craft with windows and lights
witnesses: 2 (Betty and Barney Hill)
duration: Sighting ~1 hour; about 2 hours unaccounted for
summary: Driving home to Portsmouth from Montreal, the Hills saw a light moving near the Moon south of Lancaster. It followed them through Franconia Notch, passing near the Cannon Mountain tramway. South of Indian Head it came down to about 100 ft over the road, and Barney saw figures at the windows through binoculars. They reached home around dawn, about two hours later than expected. Under hypnosis in 1964 both described being taken aboard, in the first widely publicised "alien abduction".

title: Bahía Blanca and Espora air base sightings
place: Bahía Blanca and Espora Naval Air Base
shape: Lighted "railroad car"; ball of light
witnesses: Base personnel, truck drivers, a newspaper photographer
summary: In May 1962 objects were reported at the Espora naval air base on May 11 and 18. On May 12, three truck drivers on Route 35 said an illuminated object like a railway carriage rose from a field, crossed the road at about 4 m and split in two. On May 21, La Nueva Provincia photographer Miguel Tohmé photographed an object over the city, and the photo made the front page. Sightings at the Puerto Belgrano naval base followed.

title: Socorro landing (Lonnie Zamora)
explanation: Project Blue Book listed the case as "unknown" — one of its best-known. Proposed explanations include a lunar-lander test and a student hoax; none is confirmed.
shape: Shiny egg / "O" shape on legs; red insignia
witnesses: Police Sgt. Lonnie Zamora
summary: Chasing a speeder south of Socorro, Sgt. Lonnie Zamora heard a roar and saw flame, drove toward it and saw a whitish oval object in a gully with two small figures in white beside it. The object rose on a blue-orange flame and left. Investigators found scorched brush and four depressions.

title: Big Sur — Atlas "Buzzing Bee" film
place: Anderson Peak, Big Sur, and Vandenberg AFB, California
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: Project engineer Kingston George wrote in 1993 that the film showed the re-entry vehicle releasing decoy warheads and chaff, a classified technology at the time, which Jacobs was not cleared to know about.
shape: Object circling a missile warhead
witnesses: 1369th Photographic Squadron team
summary: In 1964 an Air Force team on Anderson Peak used a telescope borrowed from Boston University to film Atlas missile launches from Vandenberg. In 1982, Robert Jacobs, the officer in charge on the mountain, said the film of one launch, nicknamed "Buzzing Bee", showed an object fly around the warhead and hit it with beams of light, and that the film had been confiscated. The project engineer said it showed decoy deployment.

title: Valensole landing
explanation: Investigated by the Gendarmerie; the ground marks and the effect on lavender plants were documented but never explained.
shape: Egg-shaped craft on legs; two small beings
witnesses: Farmer Maurice Masse
summary: Lavender farmer Maurice Masse said he found a rugby-ball-shaped craft on six legs in his field and two small beings beside it; one pointed a tube at him and he was paralysed. The craft left marks in the soil where lavender failed to grow for years.

title: Deception Island — the Antarctic sightings
place: Argentine station, Deception Island, South Shetland Islands
explanation: The Argentine Navy said in an official statement that its observers had seen a solid, lens-shaped flying object, and Lt. Daniel Perisse, at the Argentine station, said a weather balloon, a plane or a star had been ruled out. No explanation was ever published, and the photographs said to have been taken have not been released.
shape: Lens-shaped object, mostly red and green, changing to yellow, blue, white and orange
witnesses: Seventeen people at the Argentine station; nine at the Chilean station; five at the British base; two meteorologists on Laurie Island
summary: Over two winter nights in July 1965, the staff of three stations on Deception Island and of the Argentine station on Laurie Island, in the South Orkneys, reported a coloured, manoeuvring light. On July 2 five British observers saw a green and red light zig-zag, hover and speed up. On the evening of July 3, nine Chilean observers watched a light change colour and leave a steam-like trail, and at 19:42 seventeen people at the Argentine station, three Chilean visitors among them, watched a lens-shaped object. In a statement on July 6, the Argentine Navy described “a giant, lens-shaped flying object, solid in appearance, mostly red and green in color”, moving on a zig-zag course toward the east with changes of speed and direction, without sound, 10 to 15 km away. On Laurie Island, two variometers registered “sudden and strong disturbances of the magnetic field” during a 15-second sighting.

title: Buenos Aires — Meteors scrambled
shape: Two bright discs
witnesses: Many residents; Argentine Air Force
summary: Two bright discs hung motionless over Buenos Aires for about ten minutes, then flew off at high speed. With calls pouring in, the Seventh Air Brigade scrambled three Gloster Meteor jets from Morón air base, which found nothing.

title: Heflin Polaroids — Santa Ana
place: Myford Road near Santa Ana, California
explanation: Project Blue Book classed the photographs as a hoax. Analysts argued the "UFO" was a small object hung or thrown near the van. Supporters point out that Heflin's originals were never shown to be faked.
shape: Hat-shaped disc; a smoke ring
witnesses: 1 (Rex Heflin, highway traffic investigator)
summary: Orange County highway traffic investigator Rex Heflin was photographing road signs from his work van when he saw a hat-shaped object cross the road ahead. He took three Polaroid pictures through the windshield and side window, then a fourth of a smoke ring it seemed to leave behind. The photos were printed in the Santa Ana Register and studied by the Air Force and the Condon Committee.

title: Incident at Exeter
explanation: The Air Force first blamed a military exercise and twinkling stars, then changed the case to "unidentified". A 2011 Skeptical Inquirer analysis proposed a KC-97 refuelling tanker.
shape: Row of five pulsing red lights
witnesses: Norman Muscarello; officers Bertrand and Hunt
summary: Hitchhiker Norman Muscarello saw five pulsing red lights hover over a field on Route 150 and rushed to the Exeter police station. Returning with Officer Eugene Bertrand, both — and then Officer David Hunt — watched the lights rise from behind trees and move over the field.

title: Kecksburg fireball
explanation: Astronomers identified a bright bolide seen from six states and Ontario; no object was found at Kecksburg. Claims of a recovered acorn-shaped craft are unsupported, and the Soviet Kosmos 96 re-entry was ruled out by timing.
shape: Fireball; later claims of an acorn-shaped object
witnesses: Thousands across six states
summary: A brilliant fireball crossed the sky over the Detroit–Windsor area and was reported from Ontario to Pennsylvania. Residents of Kecksburg said something fell into the woods; state police and military personnel searched and reported finding nothing.

title: Tully "saucer nest"
explanation: Police and the RAAF suggested a willy-willy (whirlwind) flattened the reeds; others considered it unexplained.
shape: Grey saucer rising from the lagoon
witnesses: Banana grower George Pedley
summary: George Pedley heard a hissing sound and saw a saucer-shaped object rise from a lagoon and climb away. In its place was a floating circle of flattened, clockwise-swirled reeds about 9 m across — the original "saucer nest".

title: Michigan "swamp gas" sightings
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: J. Allen Hynek, the Air Force's scientific consultant, suggested that burning marsh gas might explain some of the lights over the swamps, and Blue Book filed the flap as "marsh gas". The explanation was widely ridiculed. Hynek later said he regretted how it was presented.
shape: Football-shaped object with lights; glowing lights over a swamp
witnesses: Farm family, a dozen police officers, 87 college students
summary: On March 20, 1966, Frank Mannor and his son near Dexter said they walked toward a glowing, football-shaped object hovering over a swamp. About a dozen police officers reported lights. The next night 87 women at Hillsdale College watched a light hover over the campus arboretum for hours. Congressman Gerald Ford called for hearings, which led to the Condon Committee.

title: Westall school sighting
place: Westall High School, Clayton South, Melbourne
explanation: Researchers have proposed a stray HIBAL cosmic-ray research balloon launched from Mildura, trailed by light aircraft.
shape: Silvery disc; descended into a paddock
witnesses: 200+ students and teachers
summary: Students and staff watched a silvery disc descend behind trees into a paddock known as The Grange, then rise and leave while light aircraft circled. Several students said they saw a flattened circle in the grass.

title: Portage County police chase
explanation: Project Blue Book (Maj. Hector Quintanilla) concluded the officers first saw the Echo satellite and then Venus; the officers and Rep. William Stanton rejected this.
shape: Bright disc-shaped light, "as big as a house"
witnesses: Deputies Dale Spaur & Wilbur Neff, officers in three towns
summary: Portage County sheriff’s deputies Dale Spaur and Wilbur Neff, checking an abandoned car on Route 224, saw a brilliantly lit object rise from the woods. Told by radio to follow it, they chased it east at up to 100 mph for about 85 miles into Pennsylvania, joined by officers from East Palestine and Conway, PA, who also saw it before it shot straight up.

title: Paulding Light
place: Robbins Pond Road, near Paulding, Michigan
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: In May 2010 students from the optics society (SPIE) chapter at Michigan Technological University watched the light through a telescope, saw that it was a pair of car headlights, and recreated it on cue by having one of them drive U.S. 45, about 4.5 miles away, with his hazard lights on.
shape: A light that brightens, dims, changes colour and seems to sway
witnesses: Visitors to the viewing spot, nightly since the 1960s
summary: From the end of Robbins Pond Road in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, visitors look north along a power-line cut and see a light rise, brighten, change colour and seem to sway before going out. Teenagers first reported it in 1966, and legends grew around it, the best known being the lantern of a railway brakeman killed on the line. In 2010 a group of Michigan Tech students set up a telescope at the spot and could make out pairs of headlights, then recreated the light on cue with a car on U.S. 45, the highway that crosses the line of sight about 4.5 miles away.

title: Malmstrom AFB Echo Flight shutdown
place: Echo Flight, Malmstrom AFB missile field, Montana
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The 1967 Air Force report found no UFO link and rumours "disproven". A 2025 Pentagon report stated the shutdown was caused by a classified electromagnetic-pulse test. Later accounts by former officers (Robert Salas) described a red glowing object over the gate.
shape: Reported glowing red object (1990s testimony)
witnesses: Launch crew; security guards (later testimony)
summary: All ten Minuteman I missiles of Echo Flight dropped off strategic alert almost simultaneously. Decades later, former missile officers said guards had reported a glowing red object hovering at the gate. The Air Force’s contemporaneous report found no UFO involvement.

title: Falcon Lake incident
place: Falcon Lake, Whiteshell Provincial Park, Manitoba
explanation: RCMP, RCAF and the Condon Committee could not explain it; some soil samples were mildly radioactive, possibly from radium paint. Later marks on Michalak’s body were judged self-inflicted.
shape: Two glowing oval objects; one landed
witnesses: Stefan Michalak
summary: Amateur prospector Stefan Michalak said two glowing craft descended near him; one landed on a rock outcrop. When he touched it, a blast of hot gas from a grid-like vent burned his chest. CBC has called it Canada’s best-documented UFO case.

title: Cussac — two children and four small black beings
explanation: No explanation has been agreed. The two children, aged 13 and 9, gave the same account to the police, and the police recorded a smell of sulphur and dried grass where the sphere was said to have stood. There were no other witnesses.
shape: Round craft about 4.6 m across, with four small black beings
witnesses: François (13) and his sister Anne-Marie (9)
summary: On August 29, 1967 a 13-year-old boy, François, and his 9-year-old sister, Anne-Marie, told the local police that while watching cows in a field at Cussac they had seen four small black beings, about 120 cm tall, with a shiny, silk-like look. The beings seemed to rise in the air and enter a round craft about 4.6 metres across that hovered over the field. The police noted a smell of sulphur and dried grass at the spot the craft was said to have left. The file is one of those that the French government put online in March 2007, and one of the children was later said to have suffered lasting health effects.

title: Shag Harbour crash-landing
explanation: The RCMP, Canadian Coast Guard and Navy divers found no aircraft; the Condon Committee listed it as unexplained. No debris was recovered beyond a yellowish foam on the water.
shape: Row of 4 orange lights; object floating on the sea
witnesses: RCMP officers, fishermen, residents
summary: Residents and three RCMP officers watched orange lights descend at an angle and hit the water off Shag Harbour. Rescue boats found a patch of yellow foam but no aircraft; no plane was missing. Earlier that evening an Air Canada crew and a fishing boat’s radar also reported unusual objects.

title: Devon "flying cross" police chase
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: The Ministry attributed it to the planet Venus, as it did several similar sightings that month.
shape: Star-spangled cross of light
witnesses: PCs Roger Willey and Clifford Waycott; a motorist; two BBC engineers
summary: Two police constables driving from Holsworthy to Hatherleigh saw a bright, cross-shaped light at treetop height. They followed it for about 14 miles, at up to 80 mph, and said it was like "looking through wet glass". A second object joined it at 04:23. A Land Rover driver saw it too. It faded at about 5 a.m. The case was raised in Parliament during the autumn 1967 "flying cross" wave.

title: Minot AFB — B-52 radar and missile-field sightings
place: Minot AFB and missile field, North Dakota
explanation: Blue Book's conclusion: ground sightings were probably the B-52 and the star Sirius; the radar contact and the B-52's temporary loss of UHF radio were "possibly plasma", similar to ball lightning; the crew's sighting could have been the star Vega or a light on the ground.
evidence: radar | military-witness | pilot-witness | photo | official-document | em-effects
shape: Large glowing orange object
witnesses: Missile maintenance and security teams; B-52 crew
summary: Before dawn, maintenance and security teams at several Minuteman sites reported a large glowing object. A B-52 returning to Minot was asked to look for it. Its radar navigator painted a target that stayed about a mile off the bomber, and radarscope photographs were taken. The UHF radio dropped out when the object was closest. After landing, the crew described a bright light near the ground. Blue Book closed it within weeks. It is one of the best-documented military cases in the files.

title: Fort Beaufort — police fire at an object
place: Braeside farm near Fort Beaufort, Eastern Cape
shape: Fireball that changed colour
witnesses: Farmer Bennie Smit, farmhands and police officers
summary: Farmer Bennie Smit said he, his workers and local police fired shots at a fireball-like object that changed colour as it hovered among the trees on his farm. The story went around the world. Rumours said the army investigated the site but no records were produced. The town's "UFO Bar" and hotel clippings kept the story alive.

title: Lake Cote aerial survey photograph
explanation: Taken by the government’s Instituto Geográfico Nacional mapping aircraft; the object was not noticed at the time. Analyses have not produced an accepted identification.
shape: Metallic disc over the lake
witnesses: None at the time (found on the negative)
summary: An Instituto Geográfico Nacional aerial-survey camera flying at about 10,000 ft photographed Lake Cote for mapping. One frame shows a disc-like object over the water that the crew never saw; the adjacent frames do not show it.

title: Delphos ring
explanation: No official body reached a conclusion. The soil results are the main physical evidence; sceptics note that the account rests on one family, and that fungi can leave rings of altered, water-repelling soil.
shape: Mushroom-shaped, with multicoloured lights
witnesses: Ronnie Johnson (16) and his parents
summary: While doing evening chores on his family’s farm near Delphos, 16-year-old Ronnie Johnson saw a mushroom-shaped object, lit in many colours, hovering about 25 yards away. His parents came out to a glowing ring on the ground where it had been. It was still visible the next day. Investigators found that the soil in the ring was dry beside damp ground and would not let water through, and that it held more calcium and soluble salts and was more acidic, with a white deposit of calcium oxalate. Both calcium oxalate and oxalic acid irritate skin and eyes, and Ronnie’s parents said touching the ring numbed their fingers. It is one of the classic UFO “landing trace” cases.

title: Pascagoula encounter
explanation: No physical evidence was found beyond the two men’s testimony. Sceptics see a hoax or a hallucination; the witnesses stuck to their story, including when they were secretly recorded at the sheriff’s office.
shape: Oval object with flashing blue lights
witnesses: Charles Hickson (45) and Calvin Parker (17)
summary: Charles Hickson and his young colleague Calvin Parker said that while fishing from a pier on the west bank of the Pascagoula River they heard a whirring noise, saw two flashing blue lights and an oval object about 30–40 feet across, and were taken aboard by three creatures with claw-like hands, examined and returned. They went to the Jackson County sheriff’s office around 11 p.m. Officers who suspected a prank left the two alone in a room with a hidden recorder; the men’s talk matched their story. The case set off a wave of 1973 reports along the Gulf Coast and made Hickson a long-time public speaker; Parker published his own account in 2018.

title: Coyne helicopter incident
explanation: The sceptic Philip Klass argued that the crew first saw a bright fireball of the Orionid meteor shower and then misjudged what followed. Investigators for CUFOS and others reject this: by their timeline the object was in view for several minutes, and a family on the ground reported lights too.
shape: Grey cigar-shaped body, red nose light, white tail light, green beam
witnesses: Four-man Army Reserve crew; a family on the ground
summary: An Army Reserve Bell UH-1H (tail number 68-15444) on its way from Columbus to Cleveland was cruising at 2,500 feet near Mansfield when the crew saw a red light closing on the helicopter from the east. Capt. Lawrence Coyne took the controls and began an emergency descent, expecting a collision. They then saw a cigar-shaped grey object hover over the helicopter, with a red light at the nose, a white light at the tail and a green beam that lit the cockpit. After it left, the crew found the helicopter at about 3,500 feet in a climb of 1,000 feet a minute, with the collective still fully down, and the compass spinning. The Army Reserve’s report is among the best-known official records of an aircrew encounter.

title: Berwyn Mountains "crash"
statusLabel: Mundane explanation widely accepted or officially assessed
explanation: A small earthquake shook the area at the same moment that a bright fireball was seen across northern England and Wales. The lights on the hillside were most likely poachers' lamps. Investigators found no crash and no recovery.
shape: Glowing light on the hillside
witnesses: Villagers across the Dee valley; a nurse who drove up the mountain
summary: At 20:38 a loud bang and tremor shook villages around the Berwyn Mountains, and people saw lights on the hillside. A local nurse drove up and described a glowing sphere. Police searched and found nothing. The event was later retold as a UFO crash with a secret military recovery, sometimes called "the Welsh Roswell". Seismographs recorded an earthquake, and meteor observers logged a fireball at the same moment.

title: Coyame “crash” — Chihuahua
explanation: Historians say the reports were most likely prompted by the crash and military recovery of a Cessna used for drug smuggling. The radar story that circulates in UFO literature is known only from later retellings.
shape: Disc-shaped object (as told)
witnesses: Local residents (reported)
summary: According to ufologists, residents near Coyame, in the Chihuahuan desert, reported a mid-air collision between a UFO and a small aeroplane on August 25, 1974, followed by a military recovery and a cover-up. The best-known version says U.S. air-defence radar followed a fast, high object from the Gulf of Mexico until it vanished near Coyame, and that a light aircraft that had left El Paso collided with it. Historians point instead to the real 1974 crash and recovery of a Cessna that had been carrying drugs, which they believe gave rise to the story. It is sometimes called Mexico’s Roswell. The case is listed because it is so often cited, not because the account is documented.

title: Langenburg rings
shape: Five domed discs
witnesses: 1 (farmer Edwin Fuhr)
summary: Farmer Edwin Fuhr was swathing a rapeseed field when he saw five metallic, dome-shaped objects spinning just above the ground near a slough. He sat frozen for about 15 minutes until they rose silently in formation and left, trailing grey vapour. He said his swather would not restart. The RCMP found five rings of flattened, swirled crop matching his description, with no tracks leading in.

title: Loring Air Force Base intrusions
place: Loring Air Force Base, Limestone, Maine
explanation: The Air Force never identified the object; its messages from the base describe an unidentified, helicopter-like aircraft that evaded the ground sweep. No conventional aircraft was found.
shape: Low aircraft with a red light and a white strobe
witnesses: Security police, including S/Sgt Danny Lewis
duration: About 40 minutes the first night; repeated for days
summary: On the evening of October 27, 1975 a security patrol at Loring Air Force Base, a Strategic Air Command base that held nuclear weapons, saw an aircraft with a red light and a white strobe approaching the north perimeter at about 300 feet. The base was put on alert and a ground sweep began. Over the next 40 minutes the object came within 300 yards of the restricted weapons storage area at about 150 feet, moving in ways described as helicopter-like, and no one could get a fix on it before it left toward Grand Falls, New Brunswick. Similar reports came from the base, and from other bases, for more than a week; Air Force messages about them were released under the Freedom of Information Act.

title: Wurtsmith Air Force Base and the KC-135 chase
place: Wurtsmith Air Force Base, Oscoda, Michigan
explanation: The NORAD log called it a helicopter over the weapons storage area, but no helicopter was identified, and the tanker crew described an object that pulled away each time they closed on it. It is one of a series of intrusions at northern Strategic Air Command bases that autumn, including Loring and Malmstrom.
shape: One white light pointing down and two red lights at the rear
witnesses: Base security police and the six-man crew of a KC-135 tanker
summary: At about 10:10 p.m. on October 30, 1975, guards at Wurtsmith, a Strategic Air Command base on Lake Huron, saw an object with a white light pointing downward and two red lights at the rear. Minutes later security police reported an “unidentified helicopter” hovering low over the weapons storage area, and the base radar approach control picked up a target about 35 miles to the south-east. A KC-135 tanker flying nearby was asked to look. Its six-man crew, among them Maj. Frederick Pappas, saw lights and painted the object on their radar for about ten seconds, and followed it at about 2,000 feet north over Lake Huron and then south toward Saginaw Bay; each time they closed in it sped away, and Capt. Myron Taylor put its final speed at about 1,000 knots. Low on fuel, they broke off. The NORAD log recorded that the tanker “made both visual sighting and radar skin paint” and that contact was lost 25 nautical miles south-east over Lake Huron.

title: Travis Walton disappearance
place: Apache–Sitgreaves National Forest near Heber, Arizona
explanation: The crew passed some polygraph tests and Walton failed one. Philip Klass and Michael Shermer argued it was a hoax, with a motive: the crew was behind on a Forest Service contract, and an "act of God" could excuse the penalty. Walton maintains it happened.
shape: Glowing disc hovering over a clearing
witnesses: 7 (the logging crew)
summary: A seven-man logging crew led by Mike Rogers was driving out of the forest after sunset when they saw a glowing disc over a clearing. Travis Walton got out and walked toward it, and the crew said a beam of light knocked him to the ground. They drove off in panic. When they came back he was gone. Police searched for five days. Walton then called his sister from a phone booth in Heber, saying he had been taken aboard. His story became the 1993 film Fire in the Sky.

title: Canary Islands sphere
explanation: Spanish researcher Ricardo Campo matched the 1976 sighting, and similar Canary Islands events of the period, to U.S. Navy submarine-launched Poseidon missile tests in the Atlantic, whose exhaust clouds glow in sunlight at high altitude. The Spanish Air Force report left it unexplained.
shape: Light rising from the sea, then a huge glowing sphere
witnesses: Several hundred, including the crew of the Spanish Navy corvette Atrevida
summary: The crew of the corvette Atrevida saw a light rise from the sea, then a vast, luminous sphere spread out in the sky. Hundreds of people across Tenerife, La Palma, La Gomera and Gran Canaria saw it. A doctor near Gáldar said he saw two tall figures inside a transparent sphere. The Spanish Air Force investigation was leaked in 1977 and officially declassified in 1994.

title: Tehran F-4 Phantom intercepts
explanation: A U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency report called it "an outstanding report" meeting all criteria for a valid study. Skeptic Philip Klass proposed Jupiter plus coincidental equipment failures.
shape: Brilliant flashing lights; object released a smaller one
witnesses: Controllers, two F-4 crews, a general, civilians
summary: After civilian reports of a bright object over Tehran’s Shemiran district, the Imperial Iranian Air Force scrambled two F-4 Phantoms from Shahrokhi AB. Both crews said their instruments and communications failed near the object; the second pilot, Maj. Parviz Jafari, reported a radar lock and that his weapons panel died as a smaller object came toward him.

title: Talavera la Real air base sentries
place: Talavera la Real Air Base, Badajoz
shape: Intense light; tall luminous figure
witnesses: 3 soldiers on guard duty
summary: Two soldiers on night patrol at Talavera la Real air base heard a sound like radio interference that became a piercing whistle. When it stopped they saw an intense light in the sky for about 15 seconds. With a third guard and a guard dog they searched the perimeter. The dog came back cowering, and they said they saw a tall, glowing figure and fired their rifles at it before it vanished. The Spanish Air Force investigated and later released its file.

title: Broad Haven schoolchildren — the Welsh Triangle
explanation: A Ministry of Defence investigator found no physical evidence that anything had landed and suggested that “a local prankster” might have been responsible. The children’s drawings agreed closely, which is why the case is still told.
shape: Yellow cigar-shaped craft; later an “upside-down saucer”
witnesses: 14 schoolchildren, then teachers and a hotel owner
duration: Lunchtime on Feb 4; further reports to April
summary: At lunchtime on February 4, 1977 a group of 14 children at Broad Haven Primary School reported a yellow, cigar-shaped craft that landed in a field beyond the school grounds, and a silver creature with pointed ears. The headmaster had them draw what they saw, and the drawings agreed closely. On February 17 teachers and others said they saw the same craft, and on April 19 the owner of the Haven Fort Hotel in nearby Little Haven reported an “upside-down saucer” and two figures in a field. The wave of sightings in the area became known as the Dyfed or Welsh Triangle. A Ministry of Defence investigator found nothing to show a landing. The events were revisited in a 2023 Netflix documentary and a 2024 BBC series.

title: Petrozavodsk phenomenon
explanation: Usually attributed to the launch of Kosmos-955 from Plesetsk, but the 1977 Academy of Sciences report said the phenomenon could not be satisfactorily understood.
shape: Glowing "jellyfish" showering rays
witnesses: Thousands, from Helsinki to Vladivostok
summary: In the early hours, residents of Petrozavodsk saw a glowing object spread over the city like a jellyfish, "raining" shafts of light. Reports came from across the Soviet Union and Finland. The event prompted the Soviet research programme Setka.

title: Colares "chupa-chupa" & Operação Prato
explanation: The Brazilian Air Force closed Operação Prato after about four months, reporting no unusual phenomena; its files and photos are in the Arquivo Nacional.
shape: Beams of light, "chupa-chupa" lights
witnesses: Islanders; Brazilian Air Force team
summary: Residents of Colares reported lights that fired beams and left burn-like marks. The mayor asked for help, and the Brazilian Air Force ran Operação Prato under Capt. Uyrangê Hollanda, photographing lights over several months. Hollanda gave a dramatic interview two decades later.

title: Emilcin abduction report
shape: White, hovering, humming craft
witnesses: 1 (farmer Jan Wolski)
summary: Jan Wolski, a 71-year-old farmer, said that while driving his horse-drawn cart through the woods near Emilcin, two short beings with greenish faces invited him aboard a white craft hovering over a clearing. There they examined him. He was later interviewed by investigators, who found him sincere. A monument now stands near the site, one of the few UFO memorials in the world.

title: Disappearance of Frederick Valentich
place: Bass Strait, off Cape Otway, Victoria
explanation: The Department of Transport could not determine the cause. Theories include disorientation (seeing his own lights reflected while inverted), a staged disappearance and suicide.
shape: "Long shape" with four bright lights, orbiting above
witnesses: Pilot (radio transcript); later ground reports
summary: Twenty-year-old Frederick Valentich, flying a Cessna 182L from Moorabbin to King Island, told Melbourne Flight Service a large lit aircraft was orbiting over him. His last words were "It is not an aircraft", followed by 17 seconds of metallic noise. No trace of him or the aircraft was ever found.

title: Clarenville — RCMP constable watches object over the water
shape: Oval with a fin, lights
witnesses: 12, including RCMP Constable James Blackwood
summary: In the early morning a dozen people in Clarenville called the RCMP about an object hovering over the water toward Random Island. Constable James Blackwood watched it for one to two hours through a surveillance telescope. He described an oval with a fin at the back, hanging about 100 ft above the water. When he flashed his headlights, the object seemed to flash back. It then vanished and left no trace.

title: Zanfretta — the Torriglia night patrol
explanation: Sceptics say the grass imprint matched the place where the owners tied a horse, that regression hypnosis can create false memories, that the beings resembled characters in popular 1978 Italian TV and comics, and that the “footprints” were puddles. Italy’s national UFO centre (CUN) judged the case unreliable.
shape: Red oval craft over 10 m across; later a triangular craft
witnesses: Pier Fortunato Zanfretta (a security guard); 52 other statements
summary: At about 11:30 p.m. on December 6, 1978 the 26-year-old security guard Pier Fortunato Zanfretta, on patrol at Marzano, in the municipality of Torriglia, noticed four lights in the garden of a mansion called Casa Nostra and then a red oval object more than ten metres across. He radioed his supervisor that “they are not men”, then contact was lost; he was found unconscious and in shock. He described three-metre beings with mottled skin, yellow triangular eyes and clawed feet. A semicircular imprint of flattened grass was found in the garden, and Carabinieri Brigadier Antonio Nucchi collected 52 statements from people who had seen strange lights that night. A neurologist found no mental disturbance in January 1979. Zanfretta later described further abductions, eleven in all between 1978 and 1981, which are the most disputed part of the story.

title: Kaikōura lights
explanation: Explanations offered include Venus and Jupiter, squid-fishing boat lights, and meteors; none accounts for the radar returns to everyone’s satisfaction.
shape: Bright white lights with a red tinge; pulsing orb
witnesses: Safe Air crew, TV crew, Wellington radar
summary: After a Safe Air crew reported lights tracked by Wellington radar on 21 December, an Australian TV crew rode along on the Argosy newspaper run. On the night of 30–31 December they filmed lights pacing the aircraft off the Kaikōura coast in colour on 16 mm film, with Wellington controllers reporting matching radar returns.

title: Cecconi G.91R photographs over Treviso
explanation: The Italian Defence Ministry later said its photo interpreters had identified the object as a cylindrical balloon made of black plastic bags (a "solar balloon"). Cecconi rejected this, noting the object did not move in his jet's wake.
shape: Dull black, capsule-shaped, with a milky dome
witnesses: Maresciallo Giancarlo Cecconi; Istrana radar; Treviso tower
summary: Returning from a photo-reconnaissance sortie in a G.91R, Italian Air Force pilot Giancarlo Cecconi was asked to identify an object tracked by Istrana radar over Treviso air base. He found a dull black, capsule-shaped object about 6–8 m long at about 1,300 m. He made passes within about 100 m and took more than 80 photographs with the aircraft's reconnaissance cameras. Then radar and the tower both lost it.

title: Val Johnson — deputy's patrol car struck by a light
